newsitem.title: UK: No big hurdles seen delaying Iraqi oil sales.
newsitem.headline: No big hurdles seen delaying Iraqi oil sales.

text.p: No major obstacles remain in the way of Iraq resuming oil sales after the food distribution plan was agreed in Baghdad between Iraq and the United Nations, foreign officials in Baghdad said.
The distribution plan is expected to be submitted to the secretary-general of the United Nations next Monday for approval.

After that a pricing formula must be agreed before oil sales can begin but that process is "unlikely to be a big hurdle" in the resumption of exports, a foreign official in Baghdad told Reuters by telephone on Tuesday.
The official noted that the pricing formula had been approved without any significant hold-up before the first tranche of Iraqi oil was sold last December.

A U.N. official said the delay until next Monday in submitting the food distribution plan to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan was due to a public holiday in Baghdad that would last until next Saturday and also because the plan had to be translated into Arabic.
On Monday Staffan De Mistura, the U.N. co-ordinator in Baghdad said "we have successfully concluded discussions in Baghdad about the new national distribution plan".

"The text now needs to be finalised and translated into Arabic. We believe the whole process will be concluded by next Monday, including the official submission by the government of Iraq to the secretary-general of the United Nations".
He declined to speculate when oil sales from Iraq might resume.
Baghdad has made the completion of an aid hand-out accord a condition for restarting crude exports under the second term of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
Oil exports under the "oil-for-food" deal between Iraq and the United Nations began on December 10 and ran initially for 180 days.
The deal was renewed from June 8 but exports have been stalled pending receipt of the new food distribution plan.
Buyers of Russian crude oil are expected to stay out of the market this week to await lower prices following news that the distribution plan had been completed.

Oil traders said they expected Iraq to be in a position to resume loadings of crude oil from the Turkish port of Ceyhan and from the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr within a week of Annan approving the aid plan.
